content: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS TIMES au NEWSLETTER SIGNUP My account Log Out Oct 21, 9:59 AM AEDT Business News Sports Technology Entertainment Health NEWSLETTER My account Log Out Australia edition Business News Sports Technology Entertainment Health Editions Australia India International Singapore United Kingdom United States NEWSLETTER Follow Us Editions Australia India International Singapore United Kingdom United States Health Healthy Living 10 Ways Seniors Can Keep Their Lungs Healthy and Breathe Easier as Respiratory Virus Season Gets Underway Vaccination, physical activity, cleaner air and managing chronic conditions can help reduce respiratory risks as flu, COVID-19 and RSV spread more widely. By Jerry Thompson Published 10/20/26 AT 4:11 PM AEDT Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Reddit Share on Flipboard Share on Pocket 10 Ways Seniors Can Keep Their Lungs Healthy and Breathe Easier as Respiratory Virus Season Gets Underway As fall turns to winter, respiratory viruses such as flu, COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, begin to spread more widely. For older adults, these infections can be especially dangerous, leading to pneumonia, hospitalization and, in some cases, death. Lung function naturally declines with age. The muscles that help with breathing can weaken, the lungs become less elastic, and the immune system may not respond as strongly to infections. Chronic conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD, asthma and heart disease can add to the risk. But health experts say there is a lot older adults can do to protect their lungs. Here are 10 tips to help seniors keep their lungs healthy. 1. Stay up to date on vaccines Vaccination is one of the most effective ways to protect against serious respiratory illness. Health officials recommend that older adults talk with their health care providers about flu, COVID-19, pneumococcal and RSV vaccines. RSV is a particular concern. The virus leads to as many as 180,000 hospitalizations a year among adults 50 and older, according to the American Lung Association. "During the 2025-26 season, RSV contributed to as many as 25,000 deaths across all ages," Harold Wimmer, president and CEO of the American Lung Association, said this month as the group launched a campaign urging older adults to discuss vaccination with their providers. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends a single dose of RSV vaccine for adults 75 and older and for adults 50 to 74 who are at increased risk of severe illness. Unlike the flu shot, the RSV vaccine is not given every year. Yet as of February, only 43% of adults 75 and older reported ever receiving one, according to the Lung Association. 2. Don't smoke, and avoid secondhand smoke Smoking remains the leading cause of lung disease, including lung cancer and COPD. Quitting at any age can improve lung health and reduce the risk of serious illness. Older adults who smoke can get help from their doctor, local quit programs or the national quitline at 1-800-QUIT-NOW. Avoiding secondhand smoke is also important, as it can irritate the lungs and worsen existing conditions. 3. Stay physically active Regular exercise strengthens the heart and the muscles used for breathing, helping the lungs work more efficiently. Walking, swimming, cycling and tai chi are good low-impact options for older adults. Federal guidelines recommend that older adults aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, adjusted to their abilities. People with lung conditions should check with their doctor before starting a new routine. Some may benefit from pulmonary rehabilitation, a supervised program that combines exercise and education. 4. Practice breathing exercises Breathing techniques can help strengthen the diaphragm and improve breathing efficiency. Two commonly recommended exercises are pursed-lip breathing, which involves breathing in through the nose and out slowly through pursed lips, and diaphragmatic, or belly, breathing. These exercises can be especially helpful for people with COPD or other conditions that cause shortness of breath. 5. Protect yourself from air pollution Outdoor air pollution and wildfire smoke can irritate the lungs and trigger breathing problems. Older adults should check local air quality reports and limit time outdoors when pollution levels are high. On poor air quality days, staying indoors with windows closed and using an air purifier with a HEPA filter can help reduce exposure. 6. Keep indoor air clean Indoor air quality matters too. Dust, mold, pet dander, cleaning chemicals and fumes from gas stoves can affect breathing. Experts recommend keeping homes well ventilated, cleaning regularly to reduce dust and mold, and using cleaning products with fewer harsh chemicals. Homeowners should also test for radon, a naturally occurring radioactive gas that is a leading cause of lung cancer. Test kits are widely available at hardware stores. 7. Wash your hands and avoid germs Simple steps can reduce the spread of respiratory infections. Washing hands frequently with soap and water, avoiding close contact with people who are sick and staying home when ill can help prevent illness. During periods of high virus activity, some older adults choose to wear masks in crowded indoor settings for extra protection. 8. Manage chronic conditions People living with asthma, COPD, heart disease or diabetes should work closely with their health care team to keep those conditions under control. Well-managed conditions can help the lungs better withstand and recover from infections. That includes taking medications as prescribed, using inhalers correctly and following an action plan for flare-ups. 9. Ask about lung cancer screening Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States, but early detection can improve outcomes. Federal guidelines recommend annual low-dose CT screening for adults ages 50 to 80 who have a significant smoking history and currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years. Older adults should ask their doctor whether screening is right for them. 10. Know the warning signs Recognizing symptoms early can help prevent serious complications. Older adults should seek medical care for persistent coughing, shortness of breath, wheezing, chest pain, fever, or coughing up blood. Infections such as RSV and flu can quickly lead to pneumonia in older adults. Early treatment, including antiviral medications for some infections, can make a significant difference. The bottom line While some decline in lung function is a natural part of aging, healthy habits can make a meaningful difference. Staying active, avoiding smoke and pollution, keeping vaccinations current and managing chronic conditions can help older adults breathe easier and stay healthier through respiratory virus season and beyond. As always, older adults should talk with their doctor about their individual health needs, especially before making major changes to their routine or if they have existing medical conditions. © Copyright 2026 IBTimes AU. content: メインコンテンツへスキップ Towards a future where we can reduce the 'anxiety' of RSV. Preventive measures to protect babies are spreading | Autumn 2026 小児医療アドバイザー 2026年10月15日 16:31 "Huh? This is clearly mild." That is what I felt recently when I saw two cases of babies under 3 months old who were infected with RSV. RSV infection in tiny babies keeps us pediatric staff on high alert. Will their breathing become difficult? Are they able to drink milk? Can they get through this without being hospitalized? It is precisely because we have been watching over them in that way that this recent impression has stayed with me. Of course, this is my personal clinical observation. One cannot judge the effectiveness of prevention based on a small number of cases. Even so, I feel hopeful about the progress in preventive measures to protect babies now. To be able to protect babies even before they are born In April 2026, the RSV vaccine for pregnant women, 'Abrysvo,' became a routine vaccination. The 'antibodies' produced in the mother's body pass through the placenta to the baby. Those antibodies protect the baby after birth from pneumonia, bronchiolitis, and other conditions caused by RSV. Being able to deliver protective power in advance to a tiny baby who has just been born. Don't you think this is a welcome change? There are also preventive methods that deliver antibodies directly to the baby after birth. Which method is suitable is discussed with a doctor based on the mother's vaccination history and the baby's condition. Note that the latest national vaccination rate for the autumn of 2026 could not be confirmed. I cannot tell you at this time what percentage of pregnant women are being vaccinated. I am paying attention to how RSV infections and the severity of cases in babies will change in the first year that this prevention has spread. "I hope the moments that cause anxiety will decrease, even if only a little." There was a case of a 10-month-old who received RSV prevention at their own expense and did not develop a fever. However, not having a fever does not prove the effectiveness of the prevention or that the case is 'mild'. What we should look at is the child's condition, including their breathing, how they are drinking, and their overall energy. While cherishing that, I hope that from now on, there will be even a little less anxiety about RSV! That is what I am hoping for. For babies to be able to spend their time more comfortably. For families to have more time to watch over them with peace of mind. I hope that progress in prevention will lead to such days. What I want to protect is their breathing now, and their breathing in the future. Here, let me share one thing I learned as a Pediatric Allergy Educator. There is a term called 'airway remodeling'. The airway is the passage for air to enter and leave the lungs. In asthma, persistent inflammation can cause the airway walls to thicken and change their structure, making it difficult for the airway to return to its original state of easy airflow. This is called airway remodeling. That is why it is important to watch over children who have repeated coughing or wheezing, connect them to appropriate treatment, and maintain a good condition. Care that reduces the 'distress' of today also leads to supporting their breathing in the future. I would like to share this perspective with those who are involved with children. It should be noted that whether RSV prevention can also prevent future asthma still requires research. Having had RSV once does not mean that a child's future is determined. When you learn, you can notice more things in your daily childcare. For example, a baby who has no fever but is not drinking as much milk as usual. Instead of just thinking, 'They don't have a fever, so they must be fine,' you gain more points to look at, such as: 'How is their breathing?' 'Is their chest sinking in every time they breathe?' 'Do they have their usual energy?' and so on. And the words we use to communicate with parents will also change. “Today, they have only been able to drink about half of what they usually do.” “They don't have a fever, but I am concerned about their breathing.” Learn. Notice. Communicate specifically. Connect to necessary medical care. Each of these actions becomes a way to protect the child. When breathing seems difficult or the child cannot drink, ensure they are taken to a medical institution regardless of whether they have a fever. Turning 'I'm glad I knew that' into peace of mind for children Because you spend every day by their side, there are small changes you can notice. When knowledge is added to that, how you watch over them and how you communicate becomes much more specific. What we want to foster through the Pediatric Medical Advisor training is exactly that kind of 'knowledge that can be used for the sake of children.' Engaging with them while looking ahead not only to their current physical condition but also to their healthy growth in the future. Let's work together to cultivate the power to protect children. The CDC expects the combined peak in hospitalizations from COVID-19, flu, and RSV to be within 20% of last season's peak, with low to moderate confidence. The update arrives as flu activity runs ahead of the usual calendar. In the week ending October 10, 5.0% of clinical lab specimens tested positive for influenza, up from 3.9% the week before, according to the CDC's FluView report, with the highest activity on the West Coast. National activity remains low overall. For households, a season like last year's still means crowded emergency rooms, missed work and school, and real danger for babies, older adults and people with chronic illness. The CDC says the outlook offers high-level information on how the season could unfold and stresses that "it is not a forecast." Putting "Similar to Last Season" Into Numbers Last season's combined peak came in the week ending January 3, 2026, according to the CDC. This year's CDC season outlook for COVID-19, flu, and RSV, published September 23, lays out what a similar season could look like for each virus. For COVID-19, modeling suggests a peak weekly hospitalization rate of 1.4 to 2.5 per 100,000 people in early to mid-January if no new immune-evading variant appears. If a variant with moderate immune escape emerges, the projected peak rises to 2.8 to 6.7 per 100,000, likely in late January 2027. About two-thirds of the experts the CDC surveyed considered that scenario unlikely. For flu, the CDC expects a moderate season across all ages, with low to moderate confidence. Last season was moderate overall but high in severity for children. For RSV, the CDC expects a peak within 20% of last season's, with moderate confidence. RSV peaked unusually late last season, in the week ending February 21, 2026, and the CDC says that may signal another late peak this season. Timing is hard to predict. COVID-19 hospitalizations usually peak in late December or early January, flu between December and February, and RSV around late December or early January. When those peaks overlap, hospitals feel the combined strain. The CDC lists several reasons the peak could run higher: a new COVID-19 variant, flu mutations that weaken immune protection, more severe strains, and lower vaccine uptake or effectiveness than last season. West Coast Flu Climbs Ahead of the Usual Calendar FluView shows activity highest in HHS Regions 9 and 10, which include California, Arizona, Nevada, Hawaii, Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and Alaska. The CDC called early-season activity higher than typical for this time of year but within expected seasonal variation. Nationally, 2.1% of outpatient visits were for flu-like illness, below the 2.9% baseline. Hospitals reported 4,024 lab-confirmed flu admissions that week, a rate of 1.2 per 100,000 people, with adults 65 and older highest at 3.8 per 100,000. No flu-related pediatric deaths had been reported for the new season, and no new human infections with novel flu viruses were reported as of October 14. Most flu viruses identified so far are A(H1N1). Early lab testing found that 94.6% of characterized H1N1 viruses, and all tested H3N2 and B/Victoria viruses, were well recognized by antibodies against this season's vaccine strains. That is an encouraging early signal, but it does not guarantee how well the vaccine will work. Elsewhere, the CDC's October 16 update said COVID-19 activity remains elevated in some regions but is declining nationally, RSV activity is very low, and rhinovirus and enterovirus, common causes of colds, are elevated. Protecting Babies, Older Parents, and Chronically Ill Relatives The CDC recommends annual flu vaccination for everyone 6 months and older, ideally in September or October. Flu vaccines prevented an estimated 180,000 hospitalizations in the 2024-2025 season, according to the outlook. For RSV, CDC's RSV vaccine recommendations call for vaccinating adults 75 and older and adults 50 to 74 who are at increased risk. Infants under 8 months can be protected through maternal vaccination during pregnancy or a long-acting antibody shot. Adults considering a 2026–2027 COVID-19 vaccine can ask a doctor or pharmacist whether it fits their age and health and how their plan covers it. Prescription flu antivirals work best when started early and matter most for higher-risk patients, the CDC says. People with fever, cough or shortness of breath should rest, stay hydrated and seek care for severe symptoms such as difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion or bluish lips. Families with an infant, an older parent or someone with a chronic condition at home may want a plan now for testing, telehealth visits and where to go after hours. Parents of young children can also ask their pediatrician whether the office offers same-day sick visits or a nurse line during peak months. The CDC says it will update the outlook if any virus shifts course, and it posts new respiratory data every Friday. For now, the agency's outlook suggests this winter will likely look familiar, and the steps that helped last season still apply. RSV IN lung transplant recipients was associated with respiratory failure, declining lung function, and mortality in hospitalized patients. An international multicenter study of 155 adult lung transplant recipients hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection identified clinical predictors of severe complications, highlighting the importance of early assessment and continued monitoring in this vulnerable population. RSV in Lung Transplant Recipients: Severe Outcomes Researchers retrospectively analyzed patients hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed RSV between 2016 and 2019 across seven transplant centers in the USA, Canada, and Australia. The median patient age was 61 years, and infection occurred a median of 14 months after transplantation. Hypoxic respiratory failure developed in 58.7% of patients, while 17.4% required mechanical ventilation. All-cause mortality within 90 days reached 7.7%. Patients requiring supplemental oxygen before infection had substantially greater odds of hypoxic respiratory failure (odds ratio [OR]: 4.81). Lower respiratory tract symptoms, including cough, chest pain, and shortness of breath, were also associated with increased odds (OR: 3.74). Older Age and Mechanical Ventilation Older age was associated with greater odds of requiring mechanical ventilation (OR: 1.06 per year), identifying an important factor when assessing hospitalized patients. Oral ribavirin treatment was associated with lower odds of mechanical ventilation (OR: 0.34). However, this association was not significant when oral and inhaled formulations were analyzed together. Oral ribavirin was also not associated with improved 90-day survival. These observational findings cannot establish treatment efficacy, particularly because prescribing decisions may have reflected differences in initial illness severity. Secondary Infections and Declining Lung Function Secondary bacterial or fungal infections developed in 33.5% of patients within 90 days. Mechanical ventilation was associated with greater odds of secondary infection (OR: 3.71). Among 61 patients with paired pulmonary function measurements, median forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) declined from 2.01 L before infection to 1.69 L afterward. Nearly half experienced reductions exceeding 10%. Graft rejection was observed in 12.3% of recipients following RSV infection. Mortality Findings Reinforce Clinical Vigilance Mechanical ventilation was strongly associated with 90-day mortality (hazard ratio: 7.79), emphasizing the severity of respiratory deterioration in this population. The retrospective design, limited number of deaths, and exclusive inclusion of hospitalized patients restrict generalizability. Outcomes also predate the availability of RSV vaccines. The findings support careful respiratory monitoring, recognition of secondary infections, and further investigation of preventive strategies to protect lung transplant recipients. Researchers retrospectively analyzed patients hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed RSV between 2016 and 2019 across seven transplant centers in the USA, Canada, and Australia. Patients requiring supplemental oxygen before infection had substantially greater odds of hypoxic respiratory failure (odds ratio [OR]: 4.81). Lower respiratory tract symptoms, including cough, chest pain, and shortness of breath, were also associated with increased odds (OR: 3.74). Older Age and Mechanical Ventilation. Older age was associated with greater odds of requiring mechanical ventilation (OR: 1.06 per year), identifying an important factor when assessing hospitalized patients. Oral ribavirin treatment was associated with lower odds of mechanical ventilation (OR: 0.34). However, this association was not significant when oral and inhaled formulations were analyzed together. Oral ribavirin was also not associated with improved 90-day survival. These observational findings cannot establish treatment efficacy, particularly because prescribing decisions may have reflected differences in initial illness severity. Mechanical ventilation was associated with greater odds of secondary infection (OR: 3.71). Among 61 patients with paired pulmonary function measurements, median forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) declined from 2.01 L before infection to 1.69 L afterward. Nearly half experienced reductions exceeding 10%. Graft rejection was observed in 12.3% of recipients following RSV infection. Mortality Findings Reinforce Clinical Vigilance. Mechanical ventilation was strongly associated with 90-day mortality (hazard ratio: 7.79), emphasizing the severity of respiratory deterioration in this population. The retrospective design, limited number of deaths, and exclusive inclusion of hospitalized patients restrict generalizability. Outcomes also predate the availability of RSV vaccines. A retrospective period-comparison study analyzed 230,333 patient-period records representing 197,630 children tested from January 2018 through December 2023. After strict pandemic controls, influenza A and M. pneumoniae rose above pre-pandemic positivity, while RSV increased chiefly among younger children and influenza B rebounded mainly in adolescents. The results describe test positivity among hospital attendees, not community incidence, and the researchers emphasized that changing testing practices and clinical case mix complicate direct comparisons. The investigators divided the six-year observation window into four periods: a pre-pandemic baseline from January 2018 through January 2020; Pandemic-I, from February 2020 through June 2021, when Guangzhou used stringent measures including lockdowns, school closures, masking and travel restrictions; Pandemic-II, from July 2021 through November 2022, when restrictions were relaxed and intermittent Omicron outbreaks occurred; and a post-pandemic period from December 2022 through December 2023, after full reopening. They tested associations using multivariable logistic regression, comparing positivity in each later period with the pre-pandemic baseline while adjusting for age, sex, inpatient or outpatient status and hospital campus. Age-period interactions were evaluated with robust Wald tests, and analyses were repeated in some form to assess the influence of repeated observations and changing denominators. Most respiratory viruses were detected less often during Pandemic-I, but the suppression was neither universal nor equally durable. Influenza A positivity fell from 19.2% before the pandemic to 5.0% during Pandemic-I, and influenza B declined from 6.5% to 0.5%. RSV fell from 21.8% to 12.3%, adenovirus from 18.4% to 1.1%, and M. pneumoniae from 12.4% to 2.2%. Rhinovirus, cytomegalovirus and bocavirus were notable exceptions to the broader viral decline. When controls were relaxed, influenza A positivity rose to 25.0%, already above its baseline, and reached 29.7% after reopening. M. pneumoniae increased more slowly, reaching 7.4% during Pandemic-II before surging to 24.1% in the post-pandemic period, the highest rate recorded for that pathogen across the four periods. Discover more Bioengineering News Subscription Bioengineering careers guide Bioengineering news subscription Bioengineering Career Guide Adjustment for the changing clinical population sharpened the principal contrasts. Relative to pre-pandemic levels, influenza A had an adjusted odds ratio of 0.23 during Pandemic-I, 1.26 during Pandemic-II and 1.52 after reopening. M. pneumoniae remained below baseline during Pandemic-II, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.54, but reached 1.99 after reopening despite a 9.3-fold expansion in the number tested. RSV produced a particularly instructive result: its crude post-pandemic positivity rate of 12.8% remained below the 21.8% baseline, yet its adjusted odds ratio was 1.31, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.06 to 1.63. Comparable-denominator analyses retained the post-pandemic increases for RSV, influenza A and M. pneumoniae, indicating that expanding testing alone did not fully account for the changes. Age-stratified models showed that these pathogen-level averages concealed substantial differences between younger and older children. RSV positivity after reopening was elevated among children aged 29 days to 23 months, with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.50, and among those aged 2 to 4 years, where the estimate was 1.86. No significant post-pandemic increase was detected in school-aged children or adolescents, while some estimates could not be calculated because of sparse events. Influenza A increased after reopening in every age group with estimable results except neonates aged 0 to 28 days. Its largest post-pandemic estimate occurred among children aged 5 to 9 years, at 1.74, followed by 1.42 among adolescents aged 10 to 17 years. Discover more Bioengineering Research Papers Learn Engineering Track Biotech Influenza B followed an unusual split between younger and older children. Positivity remained below baseline after reopening among children aged 29 days to 23 months and 2 to 4 years, with adjusted odds ratios of 0.53 and 0.58, respectively. In contrast, it increased among children aged 5 to 9 years, with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.21, and rose more strongly among adolescents aged 10 to 17 years, reaching 2.88. The difference between the overall and age-specific results was significant for all four principal pathogens, with age-period interaction P values below 0.001. M. pneumoniae showed a delayed increase concentrated in school-aged children: its post-pandemic adjusted odds ratio was 3.32 at ages 5 to 9 and 1.74 at ages 2 to 4, with no significant increase among infants or adolescents. Outpatient and inpatient sensitivity analyses indicated that care setting also shaped the apparent recovery in some pathogens. Influenza A was elevated overall during Pandemic-II, but its adjusted odds ratio in inpatients was 0.64, suggesting that the early rebound was driven primarily by outpatient testing. Influenza B remained suppressed among inpatients, including an adjusted odds ratio of 0.15 after reopening, while its strong post-pandemic increase among adolescents suggested that the adolescent resurgence was concentrated in outpatient care. Because inpatient testing was used as a proxy for more consistent clinical indications, and because testing indications were not systematically recorded, the authors cautioned that residual confounding could remain even after adjustment and restriction. Staphylococcus aureus positivity increased from 2.7% before the pandemic to 4.2% during Pandemic-I and remained at 3.6% after reopening; its adjusted odds ratios were elevated in all three later periods. Escherichia coli also had elevated adjusted odds across the later periods, while Streptococcus pneumoniae declined after reopening, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.77, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa reached 0.61. These estimates remain difficult to interpret because the composition of cultures changed markedly. Upper-respiratory specimens rose from 91.9% before the pandemic to 99.2% after reopening, while lower-respiratory specimens had much higher culture yields. Hospitalization rates, prior antibiotic exposure, specimen quality and reasons for obtaining cultures also varied, and some bacterial effect estimates reversed when specimen type was included in the model. Co-infection patterns shifted as the dominant pathogens changed. During Pandemic-I, bacterial-bacterial combinations represented 49.0% of co-infections in the study’s main analysis, a period when viral positivity was at its lowest. In a sensitivity analysis excluding dual influenza A and B antigen results, bacterial-bacterial combinations declined from 62.0% during Pandemic-I to 11.2% after reopening, while bacterial-influenza combinations increased substantially and reached 22.9% after reopening. Influenza A-B dual antigen positivity accounted for 49.7% of all co-infections overall and was particularly common among children aged 5 to 9 years and adolescents, but the investigators warned that cross-reactivity in rapid antigen testing could inflate this category. Cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus detections also required caution because they may represent reactivation rather than acute respiratory infection. The study supports an interpretation of disruption followed by non-uniform recovery, not a simple return to the old epidemiological baseline. It also cannot establish the cause of the changes. An immune gap, altered transmission, shifts in social mixing and changing patterns of healthcare use are plausible explanations discussed by the authors, but no serological or immunological measurements were collected, so the immune-gap mechanism remains a hypothesis. Other limitations include the retrospective design, restriction to two referral hospitals in one city, changing test denominators, lower sensitivity of rapid antigen assays for influenza, sparse data in some age-specific strata and differences in period lengths that prevented a strict interrupted time-series analysis. The investigators concluded that the divergent results support consideration of pathogen- and age-specific surveillance, while describing the findings as observations among tested children rather than direct measures of population incidence or evidence that any prevention strategy would prevent infection. OKALHOMA - Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is back in season, and the mother of a 4-year-old girl hospitalized with the virus is sharing the warning signs she wishes she had caught sooner. A cough that turned serious in days Marissa Deitrich said her daughter, Paisley, has been hospitalized with RSV three times this year. Each stay required oxygen. Deitrich decided to speak out about the illness because of what her family has been through. “She is a ball of energy. Nonstop. She’ll talk your ear off. She’s super outgoing.” Deitrich said. Paisley has Marfan syndrome, a condition that makes her more vulnerable to severe illness when respiratory virus season arrives. “This is her third time this year having RSV, and she’s had to be hospitalized for oxygen all three times,” Deitrich said. Deitrich urged parents to watch their children’s symptoms closely. “Even if it’s just a little cough, take it seriously because it can turn into something worse. She had a cough on Monday, a little on Tuesday, and then she was hospitalized on Wednesday,” she said. She said she hopes Paisley will be out of the hospital in a few days. Why RSV can be dangerous OU Health told News 9 that RSV can be devastating for people with weakened immune systems, older adults and newborns. Many people think of RSV as the common cold, and for most healthy people that is accurate, said Dr. Donna Tyungu, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at OU Health. “After about 6 or 7 months of age, as long as someone doesn’t have congenital heart disease or chronic lung disease, it really is the common cold for a general healthy individual,” Tyungu said. Prevention options No specific treatment exists for RSV, so doctors focus on prevention. “The only management that we really have for RSV at this point in time is prevention,” Tyungu said. Women who are 32 to 36 weeks pregnant can get a vaccine that passes RSV antibodies to the baby before the respiratory virus season, according to OU Health. Tyungu recommended that mothers who are interested contact their providers. Doctors also offer RSV monoclonal antibody injections to infants to protect against severe illness. OU Health encouraged families to talk with their health care providers about protection. Elizabeth Fitz Elizabeth Fitz joined the News 9 team in October 2024. Why? Because many insurance companies won't pay for the shots while the newborn is in the hospital. Children's Health Health insurers balk at paying for newborns' RSV immunization in the hospital October 16, 20264:46 PM ET Heard on All Things Considered Rob Stein Health insurers balk at paying for newborns' RSV immunization in the hospital Listen · 3:44 3:44 Transcript Toggle more options Download Embed Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5985001/nx-s1-9967506" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player"> Transcript Many infants are leaving the hospital without getting immunized against RSV. Why? Because many insurance companies won't pay for the shots while the newborn is in the hospital. Transcript SCOTT DETROW, HOST: There are powerful new ways to protect newborn babies against a dangerous respiratory virus known as RSV, yet many infants are still being left vulnerable. NPR health correspondent Rob Stein explains why. ROB STEIN, BYLINE: For decades, doctors and parents were helpless against RSV. The respiratory syncytial virus sent tens of thousands of newborns to the hospital each year, where they often fought for their lives in intensive care. JESSE HACKELL: Those kids can go from mildly ill to deathly ill in a matter of hours, and I've seen that happen. STEIN: Dr. Jesse Hackell is with the American Academy of Pediatrics. HACKELL: These can be very, very sick infants, and it is just something I just never want to see. There's no reason to see it. STEIN: Because three years ago, doctors finally got ways to protect babies against RSV, a vaccine for pregnant women so they can pass protective antibodies to their babies in the womb and shots of laboratory-made antibodies that shield newborns whose mothers didn't get vaccinated. HACKELL: It's been a game-changer. We have seen a tremendous decrease in the amount of both RSV illness, and there's been a huge reduction, over 60%, I believe, in the rate of hospitalization for RSV disease. And that's just massive. STEIN: But Hackell and others say far too many babies are still catching RSV. HACKELL: Only about 40% of eligible pregnant people received the vaccine during pregnancy. So that means that 60% of babies are being born without any protection. Of those 60% of babies, 40% of eligible babies were not getting protected, and that's pretty big. STEIN: RSV is still among the most common reasons babies end up in the hospital. Now, there are several reasons for this, but the big one is that many hospitals don't routinely offer the antibody shots for RSV to newborns before they get discharged. Dr. Michelle Fiscus is a pediatrician who serves as the chief medical officer for the Association of Immunization Managers. MICHELLE FISCUS: The best way to protect them is to immunize them within the first seven days of life, preferably before they ever leave the hospital after being born, because as soon as they leave, they are exposed to that virus during respiratory season. STEIN: But most insurance companies aren't reimbursing hospitals for giving the shots, which cost about $500 each. That's because hospitals typically negotiate bundled insurance payments for everything they do to deliver and care for babies, and not all babies need the shots because their moms got vaccinated or the babies aren't born during RSV season. Parents can get their babies immunized for free from a doctor's office, but Fiscus says many don't get the shot there in time. FISCUS: There's a sizable proportion of babies that do not make it to their first checkup within the first seven days of life when they're supposed to be receiving these products. And so this barrier on the commercial insurance side is causing babies to be left vulnerable. STEIN: Hospitals could offer more kids shots, say, by signing up for a federal program that provides immunizations for free. But the American Hospital Association says that program doesn't really solve the insurance nag. In a statement to NPR, the group representing commercial insurance companies, American's Health Insurance Plans (ph), says they are fully committed to providing RSV protection to babies, but they are not required to pay for the immunizations in the hospital, only in doctors' offices. content_title: 基于宏基因组二代测序解析喀麦隆国家流感监测中流感阴性鼻咽拭子的呼吸道病原谱 - 生物通
content: 基于宏基因组二代测序解析喀麦隆国家流感监测中流感阴性鼻咽拭子的呼吸道病原谱 《Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses》:Use of Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing to Investigate Respiratory Pathogens in Influenza-Negative Nasopharyngeal Swabs From Cameroon's National Influenza Surveillance 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月21日 来源:Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses 3.9 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 ORIGINAL ARTICLE Open Access 背景:在喀麦隆,国家流感监测可识别流感阳性病例,但非流感急性呼吸道感染(ARIs)的病因仍缺乏充分表征。研究人员应用宏基因组二代测序(mNGS)调查通过国家流感监测采集的流感阴性鼻咽拭子中的呼吸道病原体。 方法:研究人员分析了2023年9月至12月期间从流感样疾病(ILI)或严重急性呼吸道感染(SARI)患者中采集的199份流感阴性鼻咽拭子。制备混合DNA/RNA文库并在Illumina NovaSeq平台测序。使用METAMIC(v2.0)和SPAdes(V3.15.5)生物信息学流程进行分类学鉴定。 结果:在120/199份样本(60.3%,95% CI: 53.5%, 67.1%)中检出病毒序列,代表15种病毒。最常见病毒为鼻病毒(rhinovirus,43/131)、呼吸道合胞病毒(respiratory syncytial virus, RSV,33/131)、流感病毒(influenza virus)、副流感病毒(parainfluenza virus)和肠道病毒(enterovirus)。还检出两种非呼吸道病毒(Rotavirus和Papillomavirus)。测序平均每份样本产生2610万条读段(reads),每份样本平均深度870.3,平均基因组覆盖度(genomic coverage)82%。鉴定出11例病毒合并感染(co-infections)。还检出若干细菌和真菌属(bacterial and fungal genera)。 结论:该研究表明,mNGS为表征喀麦隆呼吸道病原体提供了强大且无偏倚(unbiased)的方法,揭示流感阴性ARI病例中存在显著病毒多样性。然而,成本和生物信息学能力仍是常规实施(routine implementation)的主要障碍。需要纵向研究(longitudinal studies)和临床相关性分析,以加强解释并指导将mNGS整合入国家监测。 论文主体解读:急性呼吸道感染(acute respiratory infections, ARIs)是全球感染性疾病相关发病和死亡的主要原因,临床范围可从普通感冒等自限性疾病到肺炎和急性呼吸窘迫综合征等严重疾病,病原包括病毒、细菌、真菌和寄生虫。喀麦隆约24%的ARI患者需要住院;在低中等收入国家(low- and middle-income countries, LMICs),可靠分子诊断工具可及性有限,ARI病因认识仍存在明显缺口。当前诊断主要依赖PCR(polymerase chain reaction),该类方法依赖已知病毒序列,难以识别意外或新发病原。喀麦隆自2007年开展流感监测,Centre Pasteur du Cameroun(CPC)为国家流感中心,每年从哨点采集约1000份呼吸道疾病患者样本,10年研究显示年阳性率为24%—29%,COVID-19扰乱了流感季节性并降低检出率。多年监测后,非流感ARI病因信息仍有限,既往研究主要依赖靶向PCR,可能漏检新发、再发、罕见或高度特异病原。因此,研究人员应用mNGS对喀麦隆流感监测中流感阴性鼻咽拭子进行呼吸道病原全面调查。该研究首次在喀麦隆应用mNGS调查流感阴性ARI病例呼吸道病原,揭示显著病毒多样性,显示mNGS作为无偏倚诊断工具的潜力,同时指出成本和生物信息学能力限制其常规应用,并建议多重呼吸道panel和纵向研究。 欢迎领域“高通量小分子筛选解决方案”>> 领 取 方法概括(不超过250字):研究人员开展横断面研究,样本来自2023年9—12月喀麦隆国家流感监测哨点(7/10行政区)的流感阴性鼻咽拭子,患者符合ILI或SARI定义;最终对199份样本进行mNGS(150份ILI、49份SARI)。湿实验室采用机械破坏、酶消化和化学裂解提取总核酸,构建DNA/RNA文库,在Illumina NovaSeq 6000测序。干实验室使用MetaMIC v2.0和SPAdes v3.15.5流程,剔除人源及非病原序列,以>10 million reads和1E-5病原读段比例阈值判定,并设环境样本和ZymoBIOMICS标准品质控。病毒阳性样本进一步组装、共识序列构建、分型及系统发育分析。 3.1 研究人群的一般特征:通过横断面mNGS分析,199份鼻咽拭子成功检测,包括150份ILI和49份SARI,采集于2023年9—12月,来自喀麦隆10个行政区中的7个;研究人群含104名女性和95名男性,年龄0—80岁,平均14.1岁;4份样本未达到10 M阈值,被判为不可解释并排除。 3.2 病毒检测与遗传多样性:通过宏基因组测序、基因组组装和系统发育分析,全部鼻咽拭子平均产生2610万条reads,平均41%来自人基因组、43%来自细菌、3%来自真菌、1%来自病毒,其余12%来自未显著匹配已知数据库的其他病毒和非病原类群。病毒reads平均测序深度为870.3,120/199份样本(60.3%,95% CI: 53.5%, 67.1%)检出病毒;组装后病毒基因组平均覆盖度为82%(5%—100%)。共鉴定11例病毒合并感染,获得131条病毒序列,包括Rhinovirus(43/131)、RSV(33/131)、Influenza virus(14/131)、Parainfluenza virus(13/131)、Enterovirus(11/131)、Adenovirus(4/131)、Cytomegalovirus(3/131)、Metapneumovirus(2/131)、Polyomavirus(2/131)、SARS-CoV-2(1/131)、Torque teno virus(1/131)、Human Coronavirus HKU1(1/131)和Epstein–Barr virus(1/131);另在2例患者中检出Rotavirus和Papillomavirus两种非呼吸道病毒。92.4%(121/131)的病毒株属于Rhinovirus、RSV、Influenza virus、Parainfluenza virus和Enterovirus五类主要呼吸道病毒。系统发育分析显示Rhinovirus遗传变异显著,鉴定23个不同亚型,分属Enterovirus alpharhino(RV-A)、Enterovirus betarhino(RV-B)和Enterovirus cerhino(RV-C);Enterovirus strains分为Enterovirus alphacoxsackie(EV-A)、Enterovirus betacoxsackie(EV-B)和Enterovirus coxsackiepol(EV-C)三血清型;Influenza strains包括5株Influenza A virus、4株Influenza B virus和5株Influenza C virus;RSV序列聚为RSV-A和RSV-B两型,以A型为主;Parainfluenza virus对应Human orthorubulavirus 4和Human respirovirus 1;其余病毒多样性较低,序列聚为单一型。 3.3 细菌和真菌检测:通过mNGS分类分析,平均43%和3%的reads分别来自细菌和真菌;细菌和真菌分别在61份和21份/199份鼻咽拭子中检出。检出的细菌包括Chlamydia pneumoniae、Corynebacterium(propinquum、efficiens、urealyticum、yudongzhengii、pseudodiphtheriticum、doosanense等)、Enterobacter hormaechei、Haemophilus(influenzae、aegyptius、haemolyticus、seminalis、caudoviricetes sp.、haemolyticus)、Klebsiella
